source.title: AlleNoise - large-scale text classification benchmark dataset with real-world label noise
source.authors: Alicja Rkaczkowska; Aleksandra Osowska-Kurczab; Jacek Szczerbinski; Kalina Jasinska-Kobus; Klaudia Nazarko

record.tranche_reason: Measures memorization and test accuracy under real-world and synthetic label noise, using a text classifier rather than the original image-classification setup.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates noisy labels, not completely random labels. It does not test shuffled pixels, independent pixel permutations, Gaussian-noise inputs, or whether networks learn real labels before random labels. It reports results for multiple methods; the rows below capture the baseline CE results and the paper's stated memorization finding relevant to label noise.
record.test_reason: The baseline text classifier tests V4's test-error component at 0%, 15% and 40% synthetic corruption. It does not establish perfect training fit or behavior through complete corruption. Validation predictions matching noisy labels measure a different construct from training-set memorization.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the evaluated noise-mitigation methods provide little or no improvement on AlleNoise, and its real-world instance-dependent errors require better approaches. The authors also emphasize the large, imbalanced category space as a potential source of difficulty.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tuned an XLM-Roberta text encoder with a classification head and AdamW on product-title classification; compared real-world and synthetic label noise, rather than fitting completely random image labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Noise type and level change the reported memorization and accuracy; test accuracy differs between clean, synthetic-noise, and AlleNoise conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: At 15% real-world noise, baseline test accuracy is 63.71%, compared with 74.85% on clean labels.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Instance-dependent human labeling errors can impair text-classifier generalization more than synthetic corruption at the same overall rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Agreement with incorrect validation labels rises during AlleNoise training, reaching up to 70%; synthetic-noise agreement is negligible or low.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Models can transfer systematic real-world labeling errors to unseen examples, unlike independent random training-label memorization.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Statistics
record.problems: The study is limited to BERT-based text classifiers and e-commerce product titles. It does not test completely random labels or report zero training error. Memorization is measured on validation examples; the headline value is described in text and plotted, without a numerical uncertainty estimate.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Table 2 contains per-method test accuracies across clean, synthetic-noise, and AlleNoise conditions; these results compare noise-mitigation methods and are not individually mapped to the claim's random-label fitting versions. Appendix B reports additional 40% synthetic-noise accuracies, but does not test the versions' defining conditions.

untested.parts: Completely random training labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and fitting under unchanged hyperparameters.
Comparative time to fit and convergence slowdown with corruption. A fixed ten-epoch budget and an approximately one-hour baseline runtime do not establish these.

Perfect training fit across corruption levels, progression beyond 40% through complete corruption, and approach to chance. The supplied text does not provide readable numerical training accuracies from Figure S2.
Controlled effects of weight decay, dropout and augmentation on random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
Temporal ordering of learning shared real patterns and memorizing noisy training labels.

record.verdict_notes: The additional synthetic-noise accuracies are explicitly declared in rows_left_out, so they are not listed as missing. Failure to measure perfect training fit or complete corruption does not justify the record's limits_scope verdict.

versions.untested_parts: Completely random labeling, zero or near-zero training error, chance test error, and unchanged architecture and hyperparameters.
Training-time cost relative to true labels and convergence rate as corruption grows.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, and Gaussian-noise inputs.

The paper evaluates 15% and 40% synthetic noise and 15% real-world noise, but does not report a single sweep from no corruption to complete corruption showing perfect training fit and steadily rising test error.
Whether regularization or augmentation prevents fitting random labels, and whether removing them alone harms true-label generalization.
Whether real patterns are learned before noisy or random labels during training.

rows.note: The paper reports the clean-set baseline accuracy for comparison with noisy datasets.

rows.subject: baseline CE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on 15% symmetric synthetic label noise; test accuracy measured on clean labels.
rows.note: The study reports reduced test accuracy under 15% synthetic label noise; it does not report zero training error for this condition.
rows.check: Accuracy falls from 74.85% to 71.97%, observing the tested test-error component. Missing training-fit evidence is an untested part, not evidence of a partial effect.

source_check.locator_found: Table 2, CE row, Symmetric and Clean set columns; Sections 4.2–4.4 establish 15% corruption and clean test labels.

rows.subject: baseline CE
rows.operation_detail: Trained on AlleNoise real-world label noise; test accuracy measured on clean labels.
rows.note: The paper says the baseline test accuracy on AlleNoise is the lowest among considered noise types.
rows.check: The numbers are correct, but instance-dependent human labeling errors do not test V4's randomly corrupted-label progression.

rows.subject: All training methods
rows.operation_detail: Measured memorizedval on validation examples with incorrect observed labels during training.
rows.value: increasing values throughout training, up to 70%
rows.note: Aggregate statement across training methods; this is validation memorization, not training error.
rows.check: This measures agreement with incorrect labels on unseen validation examples, not memorization of training labels. The 70% value is an upper extent across methods, not a common value for every method.

relationships.condition: Baseline CE on synthetic corruption, restricted to test accuracy at 0%, 15% and 40% noise
relationships.reason: R1–R2 show symmetric-noise accuracy declining from 74.85% to 71.97%; Table S2 gives 67.29% at 40%. All three asymmetric synthetic conditions also decline across these levels. This supports only the measured degradation component; the verdict additionally uses text results outside the extracted rows.
relationships.display_finding: Symmetric-noise test accuracy declined from 74.85% to 71.97% to 67.29%, and all three asymmetric conditions also declined.

relation.reason: Its baseline CE experiments directly measure the held-out-performance component of V4 across clean, 15% and 40% synthetic corruption.

tranche.reason: Provides results on degradation under synthetic label corruption in a new setting: fine-tuned XLMRoberta for large-scale product-title classification.

source_check.notes: The 40% endpoint is verified in Table S2 although absent from the listed rows. Validation noisy-label agreement measures transfer of label errors to unseen examples, not training-set interpolation.

statements.correction: XLMRoberta with CE: clean test accuracy 74.85 ± 0.15% without corruption; 71.97 ± 0.08% at 15% symmetric noise (Table 2); 67.29 ± 0.12% at 40% symmetric noise (Table S2). Code, clean controls and five-fold standard deviations reported. Supplied manuscript: preprint under review.
statements.problem: The accuracy sequence and experimental description are correct, but reviewed publication status is not established by the supplied manuscript, which identifies itself as a preprint under review.
